common_name: Smyrna Quince (Classic Large Fragrant Turkish Quince)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; quince is self-fertile and begins bearing within a few years of planting, producing hard, aromatic fruit that is typically cooked rather than eaten raw.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Smyrna is one of the classic Old World quince cultivars, originating in Turkey and long grown commercially in the eastern Mediterranean, producing large, golden-yellow, intensely fragrant fruit prized for preserves, quince paste (membrillo), and poaching, since the hard, tart flesh is rarely eaten raw. The tree is self-fertile, needing no separate pollinator, and blooms with attractive pale pink spring flowers before setting fruit that ripens in fall. Quince trees are generally low-maintenance once established, tolerating a range of soil types, though good air circulation helps reduce fire blight risk in humid climates.

common_name: Orange Quince (Classic Round Golden American Heirloom Quince)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; quince is self-fertile and begins bearing within a few years of planting, producing hard, aromatic fruit that is typically cooked rather than eaten raw.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Orange Quince is a long-established American heirloom cultivar producing large, round, golden-orange fruit with a strong, sweet fragrance, among the most widely planted quince cultivars in home orchards for its reliable production and good flavor when cooked into preserves, jelly, and paste. Like other quince it is self-fertile and needs no pollinator, blooming with attractive pale pink flowers in spring before the hard, aromatic fruit develops and ripens in fall. It tolerates a range of soil conditions and needs only routine pruning to maintain an open form that allows good air circulation, which helps reduce fire blight, the main disease concern for quince in humid regions.

common_name: Aromatnaya Quince (Russian Quince Edible Fresh Without Cooking)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; quince is self-fertile and begins bearing within a few years of planting, producing hard, aromatic fruit that is typically cooked rather than eaten raw.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Aromatnaya is a Russian quince cultivar notable among quince types for fruit that is mild and pleasant enough to eat fresh, unlike most quince varieties that require cooking to be palatable due to their hard, astringent flesh. The pineapple-yellow fruit is intensely fragrant and still excellent for cooking into preserves and quince paste, but its unusually mild, less astringent flavor when fully ripe has made it popular with gardeners who want a more versatile quince. The tree is self-fertile, cold-hardy, and otherwise managed like other quince cultivars, benefiting from good air circulation to reduce fire blight risk.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown plants in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Dwarf Everbearing stays small enough for a large container or tiny yard while still producing a long, extended crop of sweet berries.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, or grow in a large container where its compact size is a real advantage. Dwarf Everbearing is a naturally small mulberry, reaching only a fraction of the size of standard mulberry trees while still producing a long, extended harvest of sweet, dark berries over many weeks rather than the shorter few-week fruiting window of many fruit trees. Its small size makes it one of the few mulberries practical for a small urban yard, patio, or large container, and it can even be grown as a modest specimen shrub rather than needing the space of a full-sized shade tree. It fruits at a young age and requires only routine pruning to control size and shape.

planting.note: Plant in spring after the soil has warmed; Sugar Cane jujube tolerates heat and drought well and is valued for exceptionally high sugar content and crisp, apple-like texture when eaten fresh.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; jujube tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil far better than most fruit trees once established. Sugar Cane is a jujube cultivar valued for its exceptionally high sugar content and crisp, refreshing texture, similar to biting into a small, sweet apple, best enjoyed fresh at the green-to-mahogany transitional stage when both sweetness and crunch are at their peak. Fruit can also be left to fully ripen and wrinkle on the tree for a chewy, date-like texture and flavor if a different eating quality is preferred. The tree is largely self-fertile, extremely low-maintenance, and one of the most drought-tolerant fruiting trees available, making it a good fit for the hot, dry margins of a Gulf South orchard.
